module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 690

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/690](https://www.erdosproblems.com/690)
- [Er79e] Erdős, Paul, _Some unconventional problems in number theory_. Astérisque (1979), 73-82.
- [Ca25] S. Cambie, _Resolution of Erdős' problems about unimodularity_. arXiv:2501.10333 (2025).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Erdos690

/-- The set of positive integers whose `k`-th smallest prime factor is `p`: if
$p_1<p_2<\cdots$ are the primes dividing $n$ then $p_k=p$. -/
def kthPrimeFactorSet (k p : ℕ) : Set ℕ :=
  {n | 0 < n ∧ p ∈ n.primeFactors ∧ (n.primeFactors.filter (· < p)).card = k - 1}

/-- A function on the primes is *unimodular* if it first increases in $p$ until its maximum then
decreases. -/
def IsUnimodalOnPrimes (f : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ m, m.Prime ∧ (∀ p q, p.Prime → q.Prime → p ≤ q → q ≤ m → f p ≤ f q) ∧
    ∀ p q, p.Prime → q.Prime → m ≤ p → p ≤ q → f q ≤ f p

/--
Let $d_k(p)$ be the density of those integers whose $k$th smallest prime factor is $p$ (i.e. if
$p_1<p_2<\cdots$ are the primes dividing $n$ then $p_k=p$).

For fixed $k\geq 1$ is $d_k(p)$ unimodular in $p$? That is, it first increases in $p$ until its
maximum then decreases.

The answer is no in general: Cambie [Ca25] has shown that $d_k(p)$ is unimodular for
$1\leq k\leq 3$ and is not unimodular for $4\leq k\leq 20$.

The densities $d_k(p)$ exist (see `erdos_690.variants.hasDensity`), so the statement quantifies
over any function `d` recording them.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos690.lean#L2162"]
theorem erdos_690 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ k ≥ 1, ∀ d : ℕ → ℝ,
      (∀ p, p.Prime → (kthPrimeFactorSet k p).HasDensity (d p)) → IsUnimodalOnPrimes d := by
  sorry

/-- For every $k\geq 1$ and prime $p$, the set of integers whose $k$th smallest prime factor is
$p$ has a natural density. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos690.lean#L2162"]
theorem erdos_690.variants.hasDensity (k p : ℕ) (hk : 1 ≤ k) (hp : p.Prime) :
    ∃ δ : ℝ, (kthPrimeFactorSet k p).HasDensity δ := by
  sorry

/-- Cambie [Ca25] has shown that $d_k(p)$ is unimodular for $1\leq k\leq 3$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos690.lean#L2162"]
theorem erdos_690.variants.cambie_unimodal (k : ℕ) (hk : 1 ≤ k) (hk' : k ≤ 3)
    (d : ℕ → ℝ) (hd : ∀ p, p.Prime → (kthPrimeFactorSet k p).HasDensity (d p)) :
    IsUnimodalOnPrimes d := by
  sorry

/-- Cambie [Ca25] has shown that $d_k(p)$ is not unimodular for $4\leq k\leq 20$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos690.lean#L2162"]
theorem erdos_690.variants.cambie_not_unimodal (k : ℕ) (hk : 4 ≤ k) (hk' : k ≤ 20)
    (d : ℕ → ℝ) (hd : ∀ p, p.Prime → (kthPrimeFactorSet k p).HasDensity (d p)) :
    ¬ IsUnimodalOnPrimes d := by
  sorry

/-- Is $d_k(p)$ unimodular for any $k\geq 21$? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_690.variants.large_k : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ k ≥ 21, ∀ d : ℕ → ℝ,
      (∀ p, p.Prime → (kthPrimeFactorSet k p).HasDensity (d p)) → IsUnimodalOnPrimes d := by
  sorry

end Erdos690

status_issues.recorded: research open, answer(sorry). The Lean asks whether some k ≥ 21 has a unimodal d_k.
status_issues.source_status: On the erdosproblems.com forum thread for #690, on 8 May 2026, Shouqiao Wang posted a manuscript: Wang & Crapis, 'A Complete Answer to Erdős Problem 690'. Its Theorem 1.1 states that d_k is not unimodal for every k ≥ 4. It covers 4 ≤ k ≤ 8,600,001 with certified finite computations and all larger k with a uniform CRT/prime-gap construction. On 12 May 2026 Cambie commented that 'finishing the story wasn't as bad as I thought', and Nat Sothanaphan wrote 'Standard check found no issues … I think it can be regarded as correct'. The manuscript is unrefereed and AI-assisted, and was checked by two PhD students. As of the 29 Aug 2026 snapshot, the problem page's remarks still cite only Cambie. The file was added on 20 Sep 2026.
status_issues.evidence: Forum thread: https://web.archive.org/web/20260824212152/https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/690. Manuscript: https://github.com/multiscalar/results/blob/main/erdos-690/paper.pdf. Abstract: 'We prove that p ↦ d_k(p) is not unimodal for every k ≥ 4, completing the classification.' Also on the forum, Cambie (7 May 2026) says the per-k version was 'only proven for small k (up to 69)'.
status_issues.suggested_change: If the Wang–Crapis proof is accepted, change the tag to `research solved`, set `answer(False)` (no k ≥ 21 gives a unimodal d_k), and cite the manuscript. Otherwise, at least add the claimed resolution to the docstring.

reformulations.difference: The source speaks of 'the density d_k(p)'. The Lean has no density function; it quantifies over every `d : ℕ → ℝ` with `(kthPrimeFactorSet k p).HasDensity (d p)` for all primes p. It then asks for `IsUnimodalOnPrimes d`. The same pattern appears in `variants.cambie_unimodal`, `variants.cambie_not_unimodal` and `variants.large_k`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `Set.HasDensity` is a `Tendsto` to `𝓝 α` along `atTop` on ℕ, so a density is unique (`tendsto_nhds_unique`). Any two admissible `d` therefore agree on primes, and `IsUnimodalOnPrimes` only evaluates at primes. The densities exist, since the set is periodic modulo the primorial of p; this is `variants.hasDensity`, formally proved in the linked plby file. So `∀ d, hd → IsUnimodalOnPrimes d` is equivalent to unimodality of the true density function, and the implication is not vacuous. I proved the equivalence in Lean given one admissible d₀ (lemma `forall_iff`). With `answer(False)` the main statement says that for some k ≥ 1 the density function is not unimodal. That is the reading erdosproblems.com adopted when it marked the problem solved via Cambie's k = 4 counterexample.

reformulations.difference: Unimodality is weak: there is a prime mode m, f is nondecreasing on primes ≤ m and nonincreasing on primes ≥ m. It is also imposed on all primes, including the primes below the k-th prime, where d_k(p) = 0 because the set is empty. The source says 'first increases in p until its maximum then decreases'.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Cambie calls the k ≤ 3 sequences unimodal because they are 'decreasing once initial zeros are removed'. The Wang–Crapis manuscript defines unimodal as 'nondecreasing up to some index and nonincreasing after that index'. So the weak notion is the intended one. It is also necessary: d_3(5) = d_3(7) = 1/30, so a strict reading would make k = 3 non-unimodal, contradicting the source. Prepending zeros does not change weak unimodality. A mode below the k-th prime would force 0 ≥ d_k(p_k) > 0, so every mode is at least p_k, and restricting to p ≥ p_k loses nothing. Requiring m to be prime is harmless: from any real mode one gets a prime mode (the larger of the neighbouring primes' values). A strict valley still refutes the definition, as proved in Lean.

review.notes:
No misformalization found. Details:

- **Main theorem.** The main statement (`answer(False)` with a ∀k reading) matches how the source resolved the problem. Bloom marked #690 solved 'by your small k counterexamples', and Cambie describes the problem as answered 'in the negative'. Cambie's forum comment names the other reading ('for every k, is the sequence unimodular?'); the per-k variants cover it.
- **Lean experiments** (all in /workspace/review):
  - Brute-force counting over one full period with the file's `kthPrimeFactorSet` reproduces Cambie's exact appendix values (d_1–d_5 at p ≤ 11). The recursion reproduces the rest, e.g. d_4(13) = 31/5005, d_4(17) = 206/36465, d_4(19) = 1308/230945.
  - Proved: densities are unique, and the `∀ d` phrasing is therefore equivalent to unimodality of the true density function.
  - Proved: a strict valley refutes `IsUnimodalOnPrimes`, and a tie at the maximum (as for k = 3 at primes 5 and 7) is allowed.
  - An exact scan over primes ≤ 1200 finds no strict descent-then-ascent for k = 1–3. It finds strict valleys for every 4 ≤ k ≤ 20, at the same primes as the external proof's certificates, and also for k = 21 (1129–1151–1153). So the threshold 21 in `large_k` is not tight, but the statement is still correct.
- **formal_proof records.** The link is the same for all four solved declarations. It points to plby's `erdos_690` conjunction: density existence with exact values, unimodality for k = 1–3, and non-unimodality for 4 ≤ k ≤ 20. That file's `kthPrimeFactorSet` uses `0 < k` instead of `0 < n`, which is the same set because `p ∈ n.primeFactors` forces n ≠ 0. Its `UnimodalOnPrimes` and `HasDensity` definitions are identical to the file's. So it implies all four statements with trivial glue (uniqueness of limits and monotonicity of the ℚ→ℝ cast). I could not compile it or run `#print axioms` here. A grep of it and its whole transitive in-repo import closure finds no `sorry`, `native_decide` or `axiom`.
- **Minor, not a defect.** `variants.hasDensity` is essentially a textbook fact (the set is periodic modulo the primorial) but is tagged `research solved`.
- **Status of `large_k`.** The only substantive item is its possibly stale status, based on the unrefereed May 2026 Wang–Crapis manuscript. I did not verify that proof.
